newsitem.title: USA: Dollar benefits from French vote, but risks remain.
newsitem.headline: Dollar benefits from French vote, but risks remain.

text.p: The dollar gained as a swing to the left in first-round French elections heightened prospects for a weak euro, but fears of an eventual delay to the timetable for a single currency restrained dollar bulls.

"The short-term is somewhat bullish for the dollar because this feeds on the notion in the market that a strong mark will be replaced by a weak euro," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
A strong left-wing showing in the Sunday polls prompted worries that strict European economic and monetary union (EMU) entry rules could be bent to fit political wishes.

France's opposition socialist party, which looks set to wrest power from the ruling right-wing coalition in the second round of elections on June 1, supports EMU but places heavy emphasis on growth and jobs. It also wants Italy and Spain to join EMU in the first wave of membership in 1999.
However, some analysts were cautious as the dollar rose above 1.70 marks, saying relaxed entry criteria would greatly increase the risk of a delay to the EMU timetable.

"If (the French) indicate they would miss the budget deficit-to-GDP (Gross Domestic Product) criteria by more than 0.5 (of a percentage point), so the ratio is above 3.5 percent, that would make it difficult for Germany to swallow EMU happening on time," said Steven Brice, foreign exchange analyst at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
"If this does snowball, we could see dollar/mark down to 1.66 this week," he added.
The dollar rose to 1.7000/10 at midday on Tuesday, up from 1.6925/35 in late trading Friday and 1.6860/70 at Monday's close.

The reaction to the election results in Monday trade was mixed. The mark initially pushed higher against the French franc as dealers expected a left-wing government would be less severe on budget cuts. But speculation of a broader-based EMU quickly drove the German unit back down, dealers said.
Also bolstering the dollar on Tuesday was market talk that Germany was aiding the French franc at the expense of its own currency by easing the German call money rate, dealers said.

"Short-term (the election results) are good for dollar/mark because it looks like given the pressures on the franc coming out of it, Germany is helping out with easier money," said Andrew Hodge, financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert.

"The Bundesbank is using that technique to take some pressure off the franc and it's working pretty well. The franc on the mark cross and other crosses is not reacting as unfavorably as had been expected," he added.
Many dealers were short French francs going into Sunday's vote and were disappointed with their return.
"We were short French francs going into this. We didn't get as much as we would like because the Germans helped out," said a currency trader at a European bank here.
Analysts did not think Germany would go so far as to lower the repo rate or other official short-term interest rates to support the franc.
"I doubt they are ready to cut the repo or discount rate, but certainly if they are being a little generous in the bond market -- it is more than just a little coincidental," Gilmore said.
